name: Taulagi — now carded as Heisuke, Muken's Last Soldier
body: Compact and dense, not tall — 'built out of the same short heavy timber the frontier built everything out of.' Sun-cured brown skin weathered to worked leather by forty-plus years above the treeline in polar wind. Iron-grey hair in a single heavy knot, close-trimmed beard sized to sit under a gorget, Moto military grooming. A tatau genealogy runs wrist to elbow on the left forearm, marking service, kills, and the names of men he failed to bring home. Wears brigandine conformed to his body over decades; carries a plain, uninscribed, obsessively maintained steel sword and distrusts Aetheric fixes for physical problems.
energy: Low and banked. Even at his king's daughter's reunion — arguably the most charged moment in either scene — his only externalized response is a hand rising partway to his chest and stopping, and a chin lifting a quarter inch. No flare, no waste.
register: Plain frontier-military register: declarative, procedural, unornamented. A report-and-observation voice, not a persuading or storytelling one. Etiquette-bound — he has a stated rule for when he is permitted to speak at all.

evidence.quote: Iron-grey hair bound in a single heavy knot at the crown, the Moto military style. Beard trimmed close enough to sit beneath a gorget. Skin dark brown and weathered to worked leather by decades in polar wind.

evidence.source: wiki/Volume I — Character Cards/Heisuke — Muken's Last Soldier.md:23
evidence.quote: The sword at his hip is not inscribed. It is steel. Good steel, Stannvaard-forged, maintained with obsessive regularity. He does not trust Aetheric solutions to physical problems.

evidence.source: wiki/Volume I — Character Cards/Heisuke — Muken's Last Soldier.md:24
evidence.quote: Heisuke has not spoken to Sodoku since boarding. He will speak when Sdoku requires it and not before, because Heisuke understands the etiquette of a man returning to claim a throne: the throne is not yet his.

evidence.source: wiki/Volume I — Character Cards/Heisuke — Muken's Last Soldier.md:29
evidence.quote: He held no position in the exile. He held the memory. The memory was the position.

Heisuke had not spoken since Stormfold. Sixty-one years old, built out of the same short heavy timber the frontier built everything out of, with the sun-cured brown skin of a man who had spent forty years outdoors above the treeline and a face that had settled into an expression of patient refusal sometime around the assassination and had not moved since. His hand had come partway to his chest. It stopped at the sternum and stayed.
Heisuke said nothing. He lowered his hand, and the set of his mouth did not soften, and he did not step back either.
Heisuke had seen it too. The old man's chin had come up perhaps a quarter of an inch.
Heisuke's hands stayed exactly where they were.

reference_direction: Male, low register — not deep bass, but low and sitting under the chest rather than at the front of the mouth. Texture is dry and grated: forty-plus years talking into cold, dry wind above the treeline, so a fine constant rasp rather than a growl or a boom. Pace is heavily rationed — long holds before a sentence starts, short sentences once they do, as if every word was checked for waste before being spent; he has gone entire scenes, including his king's daughter's reunion in front of him, without saying one word aloud. Accent flavour: plain frontier-outpost plainness, no polish, no lilt, no rhetorical shape — an issuer of reports and orders, not a talker. Closest comparison: an old high-altitude border sentry or watch-captain, the type whose decades of near-silence at a frontier post have made restraint itself the loudest thing about him.
accent_hint: Plain frontier/border-guard flavour — no polish, no urban lilt, no real-world national accent attached; a northern-outpost register general to the Kharven-Moto frontier culture, not any specific real ethnicity.
one_line: A compact, iron-grey border-guard of sixty-one winters who does not say a single word aloud in either scene he appears in — dry, low, wind-cured, and rationed almost to muteness.
